questions.stem: A natural hazard differs from an ecological hazard because a natural hazard:
options: is always caused directly and deliberately by people
arises from atmospheric, geological or hydrological processes
arises from living organisms such as pests, weeds and diseases
only ever affects places where no people live or work
questions.explanation: Natural hazards include bushfires, floods, cyclones and earthquakes. Ecological hazards come from biological processes, such as invasive species, disease outbreaks or algal blooms.

questions.stem: Two towns face the same bushfire threat, but one has older residents, no fire breaks and a single road out. In hazard terms, that town has higher:
options: vulnerability, which raises its overall risk
magnitude, which makes the fire itself larger
frequency, which means fires happen more often
resilience, which lowers its overall risk
questions.explanation: Risk depends on the hazard and on vulnerability, the characteristics that make people and places more likely to suffer harm. Mobility, preparation and escape routes all affect vulnerability.

questions.stem: Large, intense bushfires that burn hundreds of thousands of hectares occur less often than small grass fires. This illustrates the relationship between:
options: weathering and erosion
birth rate and death rate
magnitude and frequency
latitude and longitude
questions.explanation: For most hazards, high-magnitude events are rarer than low-magnitude ones. Planning uses this relationship to decide what size of event to prepare for.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four phases of emergency management used in Australia?
options: prevention, prosecution, repair and review
prevention, preparedness, response and recovery
prediction, protection, rescue and rebuilding
planning, protest, response and relocation
questions.explanation: The PPRR model covers actions before (prevention and preparedness), during (response) and after (recovery) a hazard event.

questions.stem: Bushfires are common in regions with Mediterranean climates, such as southern Australia, California and southern Europe. The main reason is that these regions have:
options: no vegetation at all, so there is nothing to stop fires spreading
hot, dry summers that dry out vegetation grown in wetter seasons
high rainfall in every month that keeps all vegetation green
permanent snow cover that prevents vegetation from growing
questions.explanation: Fuel grows in the wetter season and then dries during long, hot, dry summers, creating ideal fire conditions. Fires need fuel, so treeless deserts and wet climates burn less.

questions.stem: In an average year, the largest area burnt in Australia is in the tropical savannas of northern Australia, mostly in the dry season. Why are these fires less destructive to people than many in the south-east?
options: they burn only during the wet season when it rains
northern Australia has no vegetation that can burn
they only burn in towns that have fire stations
they mainly burn grass in sparsely populated areas
questions.explanation: Savanna fires burn widely through grasses each dry season but mostly away from large populations. South-eastern forests near towns and cities can produce intense fires that threaten many people and homes.

questions.stem: The 'fire triangle' shows that a fire needs:
options: fuel, oxygen and heat
fuel, water and a strong wind
rain, heat and smoke
oxygen, ash and soil
questions.explanation: A fire burns only when fuel, oxygen and a heat source come together. Removing any one, such as fuel through hazard reduction, can stop or slow a fire.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions produces the most dangerous bushfire weather in south-eastern Australia?
options: heavy rain, cool temperatures and calm, still conditions
high humidity, fog and light winds from the ocean
high temperatures, low humidity and strong north-westerlies
low temperatures, high humidity and light south-easterly winds
questions.explanation: Hot, dry, gusty winds from the inland dry fuels and drive fires rapidly. A southerly change can then swing the fire front, widening its path.

questions.stem: Fires usually spread faster up a slope than down it. Why?
options: vegetation on slopes contains more moisture
smoke blocks oxygen from reaching downhill fuel
flames lean towards the fuel above, preheating it
air is always colder near the top of a hill
questions.explanation: On an upslope the flames lean towards unburnt fuel, drying and heating it so it ignites more easily. Rate of spread roughly doubles for every 10 degrees of upslope, a common rule of thumb.

questions.stem: The Bureau of Meteorology recorded 2019 as Australia's warmest and driest year on record. How did this influence the 2019-20 fires?
options: it reduced the amount of fuel, so fires were smaller
it caused heavy rain that slowed the spread of fires
it had no effect, because fires depend only on wind
it left fuels and soils extremely dry over large areas
questions.explanation: Record heat and prolonged drought dried forests that do not normally burn so extensively, making huge areas available to fire at once.

questions.stem: In 2019 a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole was one of the climate drivers behind the drought in south-eastern Australia. How does a positive IOD usually affect the region?
options: cooler water near Australia reduces moisture and rainfall
warmer water near Australia brings above-average rainfall
it causes tropical cyclones to form over south-eastern NSW
it has no effect on Australian rainfall in any season
questions.explanation: In a positive IOD, cooler sea temperatures off north-western Australia mean less moisture is carried across the continent, reducing winter and spring rainfall in the south-east.

questions.stem: Some of the Black Summer fires generated pyrocumulonimbus clouds. Why are these fire-generated thunderstorms so dangerous?
options: they always bring heavy rain that floods the fire ground
they cool the air and stop fires from spreading further
they form only over the ocean, away from any fire front
they cause erratic winds and lightning that start new fires
questions.explanation: Intense heat drives smoke and air high into the atmosphere, forming storm clouds that produce gusty, unpredictable winds, lightning and ember attack, making the fire behaviour extreme.

questions.stem: The NSW Bushfire Inquiry found that most of the area burnt in NSW in 2019-20 came from fires started by:
options: power lines
lightning
arson
campfires
questions.explanation: Dry lightning storms started most of the fires that burnt the largest areas, including the Gospers Mountain fire, which burnt about half a million hectares. Arson contributed a small share of the area burnt.

questions.stem: Scientists expect climate change to lengthen fire seasons in south-eastern Australia. Which evidence best supports this?
options: a fall in the number of people living in fire-prone areas
a long-term rise in dangerous fire weather days since the 1950s
a single severe fire season that burnt more area than any before
the number of fire trucks owned by each state fire service
questions.explanation: Fire weather indices built from temperature, humidity, wind and dryness show more dangerous fire weather days and earlier starts to the season over decades. One extreme season alone cannot show a trend.

questions.stem: Which human activity most increases the exposure of people and property to bushfire?
options: planting crops on cleared, irrigated farmland
building high-rise apartments in the inner city
expanding public transport in the central city
building homes in bushland on the urban fringe
questions.explanation: Housing in the wildland-urban interface places people and assets next to flammable vegetation. Inner-city development is far less exposed.

questions.stem: Which is an example of human activity directly igniting bushfires?
options: a dry lightning storm passing over a forest
a heatwave following a long drought
strong winds ahead of a cold front
sparks from machinery or faulty power lines
questions.explanation: People start fires through arson, escaped burns, machinery and electrical faults. Lightning, heat and wind are natural factors, though human-induced climate change affects heat and drought.

questions.stem: The NSW Bushfire Inquiry reported that the 2019-20 fires in NSW burnt about:
options: 55 000 hectares
550 000 hectares
55 million hectares
5.5 million hectares
questions.explanation: About 5.5 million hectares burnt in NSW, roughly 7% of the state, and more than 2 400 homes were destroyed. Across Australia, the total area burnt was much larger.

questions.stem: Smoke from the Black Summer fires blanketed Sydney and Canberra for weeks. This is best classified as which type of impact?
options: a political impact on electoral boundaries
a social impact on health and wellbeing
an economic impact on export prices
a geomorphic impact on river channels
questions.explanation: Poor air quality caused breathing problems, hospital admissions and deaths, especially among vulnerable people. Smoke also had economic effects, such as lost tourism and work days.

questions.stem: Heavy rain soon after the fires washed ash and sediment from burnt catchments into rivers, causing fish kills. This is an example of:
options: a primary impact caused directly by the flames
a preparedness measure taken before the fire
a positive impact of fire on water quality
a secondary impact on natural systems
questions.explanation: Without vegetation, soils erode and ash enters waterways, lowering oxygen levels and harming aquatic life. These secondary impacts can last long after the fire is out.

questions.stem: Tourism businesses on the NSW South Coast lost much of their summer trade in 2019-20 because visitors left or stayed away. This shows that bushfire impacts are:
options: economic as well as environmental
limited only to the area actually burnt
restricted to damage to native vegetation
felt only by people whose homes burnt
questions.explanation: Road closures, evacuation and fear of fire cut visitor numbers, harming businesses that were not directly burnt. Impacts spread through economic links.

questions.stem: Many eucalypts resprout after fire, but the Black Summer fires burnt some rainforest and alpine areas that rarely burn. Why is this a concern?
options: rainforest and alpine plants grow back faster than eucalypts
fire improves rainforest soils so they hold more water
these ecosystems are poorly adapted to fire and may not recover
these ecosystems need fire every year to survive and reproduce
questions.explanation: Fire-adapted eucalypt forests recover, but rainforests and alpine communities lack those adaptations. Repeated or unusually intense fire can shift them permanently to other vegetation types.

questions.stem: Hazard reduction burning aims to reduce bushfire risk by:
options: rebuilding homes after a fire has passed
lowering fuel loads before fire seasons
putting out fires once they have started
evacuating residents during an emergency
questions.explanation: Planned, cooler burns in suitable weather reduce the fuel available to a later fire, making it less intense and easier to control. It is a prevention measure.

questions.stem: A family writes a bushfire survival plan, clears gutters and decides in advance when they will leave. These actions belong to which phase of management?
options: recovery
risk transfer
preparedness
response
questions.explanation: Preparedness actions get people ready to act during an emergency. Response is what happens while the fire is burning, and recovery follows it.

questions.stem: In 2022, Australia introduced a new national Fire Danger Rating System. Its four levels are:
options: Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic
Low, Medium, Very High, Severe and Code Red
Green, Amber, Orange and Black
Watch, Advice, Warning and Danger
questions.explanation: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System simplified the earlier scale to four levels with clear actions for each. Warning levels for individual fires (Advice, Watch and Act, Emergency Warning) are a separate system.

questions.stem: Fire-prone parts of NSW require new homes to be built to a standard based on their Bushfire Attack Level. This response works mainly by:
options: reducing buildings' vulnerability to embers and heat
preventing lightning from igniting fires near new homes
guaranteeing that no home will ever be damaged by fire
removing the need for residents to plan for bushfire
questions.explanation: Higher attack levels require features such as ember screens, non-combustible materials and toughened glass. These reduce but do not eliminate the chance of a home being destroyed.

questions.stem: Which is an example of bushfire management at the national scale?
options: a household clearing leaves from its gutters before summer
a local brigade running a community fire safety meeting
a council slashing grass along one road verge
a royal commission into national disaster arrangements
questions.explanation: The Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements, held after Black Summer, looked at national coordination, aerial firefighting and warnings. The other actions are household or local.

questions.stem: The NSW Rural Fire Service's Fires Near Me app shows fire locations and warning levels on a map. Its main contribution to management is:
options: replacing the need for any firefighters on the ground
predicting the exact location of every lightning strike
giving residents timely information on when to leave
putting out fires automatically using satellites
questions.explanation: Spatial technologies and apps help people act early, which reduces deaths. Warnings rely on people understanding and acting on them.

questions.stem: Firefighters establish containment lines and residents evacuate to an evacuation centre as a fire approaches. These actions belong to which phase of management?
options: response
prevention
recovery
mitigation planning
questions.explanation: Response covers actions taken while the hazard is happening, such as firefighting, warnings and evacuation. Recovery follows the event, and prevention happens well before it.

questions.stem: After the fires, agencies mapped the extent and severity of burning across NSW. Which data source is best suited to this task?
options: satellite images taken before and after the fires
interviews with a small number of local residents
a single ground photograph taken at one town
rainfall totals recorded at one weather station
questions.explanation: Comparing satellite images before and after fire shows the burnt area and, using changes in vegetation reflectance, how severely it burnt. Interviews and single photos cannot map millions of hectares.

questions.stem: After Black Summer, some groups called for much more hazard reduction burning, while some ecologists urged caution. Which concern best explains the ecologists' view?
options: burning too often harms biodiversity and has limits in extreme weather
hazard reduction burning always increases the fuel load in forests
planned burns are never carried out by fire agencies in NSW
fire has no role in any Australian ecosystem, so burning is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Burning too often can reduce plant and animal diversity, and studies suggest reduced fuel has less effect on fire spread in catastrophic conditions. Most experts support targeted burning near assets.

questions.stem: A farmer, an insurance company and a city resident hold different views on who should pay to rebuild after a bushfire. In geographical inquiry, these are best treated as:
options: scientific facts that settle the question of responsibility
irrelevant opinions that have no bearing on management
varying perspectives shaped by interests and values
errors that should be removed before analysing the hazard
questions.explanation: Stakeholders see hazards through their own interests, such as livelihoods, costs or lifestyle. Understanding these perspectives helps evaluate whether management is fair and effective.

questions.stem: The NSW Bushfire Inquiry found that firefighting saved many homes but that the scale of the 2019-20 season overwhelmed resources at times. Which evaluation is most balanced?
options: response was completely ineffective, as nothing was saved anywhere
response was irrelevant, because fires stopped on their own in spring
response was partly effective, but extreme conditions exposed limits
response was completely effective, as no homes or lives were lost
questions.explanation: Thousands of homes were defended successfully, yet more than 2 400 were lost and lives were lost. Effectiveness should be judged against the severity of conditions and what was achievable.

questions.stem: Which criterion would be most useful for evaluating the effectiveness of warnings during the Black Summer fires?
options: whether residents received and acted on warnings in time
the number of television channels that reported the fires
the total cost of fire trucks bought in the previous year
the height of the tallest trees in the burnt national parks
questions.explanation: Warnings are effective only if they reach people, are understood and lead to timely action. Inquiries examined these questions using surveys and records.

questions.stem: After Black Summer, the NSW Government accepted all 76 recommendations of its Bushfire Inquiry. Why is this alone not enough evidence that management has improved?
options: accepting recommendations always makes the next fire season more severe
no inquiry recommendation has ever been acted on by any NSW government
effectiveness depends on recommendations being carried out and working
the recommendations were about flood management, not about bushfire
questions.explanation: Accepting recommendations shows intent, but evaluation needs evidence that they were funded, implemented and improved outcomes in later events.

questions.stem: Which recovery action best builds resilience for future bushfires, not just repairing damage?
options: removing all firefighting resources once the fires are out
abandoning bushfire planning because fires are unpredictable
rebuilding to higher standards and relocating exposed homes
rebuilding every home exactly as it was in the same location
questions.explanation: 'Building back better' reduces vulnerability through stronger construction, better siting and community preparedness. Rebuilding identically recreates the same risk.

questions.stem: A student compares the management of the Black Summer fires with a bushfire event in California. Which comparison is most useful geographically?
options: which fire had the more dramatic photographs in the news
which country has the hotter capital city in winter
how planning, warnings and resources affected outcomes
which country has the larger total land area and population
questions.explanation: Comparing the same hazard in two places shows how governance, resources, building rules and community preparation shape impacts and responses, which can be applied to other contexts.
